title: Many People Aren’t Connecting the Dots Between Climate Change and Extreme Weather
text:
At the end of August, devastating floods and a debris flow triggered by a glacier collapse crashed through the valleys of Nepal, killing more than 1,300 people. Earlier this summer, deadly heat waves plagued much of the United States and Europe. Meanwhile, record-low snow levels and a long-term drought stoked wildfires across the western U.S.
It’s been a relentless summer of extremes—only the latest in a half-decade packed with record-breaking weather events. A growing body of research shows they’re becoming more frequent and severe as human-caused climate change accelerates.
But recent studies show that many people aren’t making this link in the wake of a weather disaster, a disconnect that could affect our ability to combat worsening warming. At the same time, a recent analysis found that fewer journalists are doing the kind of climate reporting that could help to close this gap. And even when hurricanes, wildfires or floods get widespread attention, it’s often not long before another story overwhelms the news cycle.
The good news: Scientific understanding of climate change and its impact on extreme weather is the best it’s ever been. But experts warn if people remain in the dark about these climate connections, it will be more difficult to prepare and adapt.
Understanding the Disconnect
For decades, scientists have been trying to grasp how people perceive extreme weather in the context of climate change. Dozens of studies, surveys and models seem to support only one consensus: It’s complicated.
“Most people do not automatically, intuitively, on their own, connect that event—a flood, a heat wave, a wildfire—to climate change,” Anthony Leiserowitz, the director of the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication, told me. “Climate change is still a relatively abstract idea for many, many people.”
Whether someone makes the connection depends on a variety of factors, from their socioeconomic background to their political affiliation. For a 2019 study, researchers analyzed 73 papers that focused on the relationship between climate change experiences and public opinion. The results were mixed. Several studies supported at least some association between weather experiences on people’s climate opinions, while others found little to no impact. A major takeaway of the 2019 paper is that different methodologies across the research make direct comparisons challenging.
More recent studies suggest that the type of extreme weather can also play a part. A 2024 study found that fires were the only type of climate-fueled weather events to have a small but significant effect on individuals acknowledging the existence of global warming and supporting the need for action (even then, the impact was short-lived). Separate research co-authored by Leiserowitz found that more exposure to hot, dry days significantly increases Americans’ perceptions that they have personally experienced global warming. Individuals did not make the climate link with heavier rainfall, though.
Leiserowitz said one barrier preventing individuals from associating weather events with the warming that is often fueling them is something called “psychological distance.” That’s essentially a person’s perception of how much something hits home—literally and figuratively.
“In general, people are more concerned about things that are happening to them or to their loved ones than they are people or species or places on the other side of the planet that they’ve never been to [and] they don’t have any connection to,” Leiserowitz said. Pointing to the recent floods in Nepal, he added: “For most Americans, they’ve never been to Nepal. They don’t know anyone from Nepal. They don’t have any connections in Nepal. They probably couldn’t identify Nepal on a map.”
The long-term timescales of climate change can also distance a person from its impacts in the present, he said.
Unraveling how the perception of climate change following extreme weather can influence government policies, meanwhile, comes with its own set of complexities.
“Getting somebody to change their light bulb is totally different than getting them to pack an emergency go kit, which is very different than helping them buy an electric vehicle, which is very different than putting pressure on their elected officials to take greater action,” Leiserowitz said.
A “Teachable Moment”
An extreme weather event is often devastating, taking lives and a serious financial toll. From a climate communication standpoint, though, it can also act as a “teachable moment,” Leiserowitz said.
“Suddenly, the public, the media and political leaders all focus their very scattered and limited attention on the same event,” he said. “A lot of this is just about helping people connect the dots for the very first time. And once you’ve done that, you’ve taught them something, and they are now primed to make that connection themselves in the future.”
That’s where the media can come into play. A 2025 report drawing from survey data across eight countries found “strong agreement that climate news coverage is important,” though only around four in 10 said the news media does a good job explaining causes and offering solutions. A June study focused on European online news media found evidence that climate news in national outlets increases public concern about climate change.
However, as climate change impacts are worsening, coverage of them is dwindling. University of Colorado Boulder’s Media and Climate Change Observatory recently found that global news coverage of the topic has decreased by 38 percent since its peak in 2021. The authors pointed to a number of possible causes, including the avalanche of other news in recent years—from war to the Trump administration dismantling federal policies. Newsrooms such as The Washington Post and NPR have also downsized their climate reporting teams or focused on other beats, potentially to avoid “climate fatigue” among their audience, as Grist reports.
But this climate coverage cliff could leave people in the dark about crucial information, according to analysis co-author Max Boykoff, professor of environmental studies at the University of Colorado Boulder.
“People typically do not start their day with a cup of coffee and the latest peer-reviewed journal article. Instead, they turn to media—television, newspapers, radio, social media—to understand how science and policies could impact their everyday lives,” he told the university. “When the media fail to cover these pressing climate issues abundantly and accurately, people may not recognize how climate change shapes their daily lives, livelihoods and challenges.”
As my colleague Bob Berwyn recently reported, climate attribution science has advanced tremendously in recent years, which experts say could help communities understand and adapt to intensifying extremes. But ensuring that information reaches these communities is a different story.
“If you don’t know about climate change, you can’t make decisions knowing that the events that you’re already experiencing are going to become more frequent, more severe, and there’s going to be more surprises,” Leiserowitz said. “Now, if you understand that, you can start to take actions to both mitigate the risk to reduce and limit climate change, but you can also be taking the incredibly important actions now that are about preparing for and adapting to that future world.”

More Top Climate News
The Trump administration proposed a rule on Friday that could leave vast swaths of U.S. wetlands with fewer protections, Maxine Joselow reports for The New York Times. The Environmental Protection Agency and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers are seeking to narrow the definition of “waters of the United States” that are protected under the Clean Water Act of 1972. While farming interests celebrated the move, environmentalists warn that it would threaten drinking water and wildlife habitat. Wetland ecosystems are already under threat from climate change, as Madeline Shaw recently reported for ICN.
Drought is impacting black bears’ food supplies in the Mountain West region of the U.S., forcing the animals closer to humans as they seek sustenance, Brittany Peterson and Mead Gruver report for The Associated Press. Past research has found that climate-fueled droughts are increasingly forcing bears, bobcats and pumas closer to people and increasing the risk of human-wildlife conflict.
Israel’s national water company says that a microalgae bloom in the Mediterranean Sea is responsible for temporarily inhibiting five of the country’s six coastal desalination plants, Laura Paddison reports for CNN. These types of facilities —which typically convert ocean water into potable supplies—provide at least 65 percent of the country’s drinking water. However, algae can damage the equipment. The desalination plants have at least partially come back online, but experts fear this type of rare event could happen more frequently as ocean temperatures warmed by climate change fuel algae blooms.

title: The Winners and Losers of Maine’s Race to Armor Its Shoreline Against Climate Change
text:
GORHAM, Maine—Supersonic shockwaves shook the bones of Charlie Hamblen’s historic Maine farmhouse more than a dozen times last year, travelling over half a mile from blasts at a nearby quarry.
The quarry is one of two active in Gorham, a vibrant and growing town of nearly 20,000 residents a few miles west of Portland, and its frequent blasts are emblematic of a broader trend spanning Maine in recent years: The state’s construction aggregate industry is booming, thanks at least in part to climate change, as property owners erect or repair stone walls to protect against sea level rise, flooding and erosion.
The number of permits to develop new quarries have more than tripled in Maine over the past five years compared to the prior decade, according to the Maine Department of Environmental Protection. Meanwhile, quarry owners in Gorham and beyond are looking to expand their existing pits, potentially bringing more Maine residents into the pathway of the quarries’ shockwaves.
“If they expand this quarry, we figure it’s going to impact at least another 300 existing houses, let alone the new houses being built,” said Hamblen.
The growth in quarries coincides with trends in Maine and elsewhere in New England, including steady increases in construction and recurring annual road maintenance needs, but also the climate-amplified boom in stone walls.
After a trio of destructive winter storms inundated the central Maine foothills and slammed into the coast two years ago—illuminating the state’s vulnerability to similar climate change-fueled storms—the number of permit applications for seawall projects skyrocketed, expedited by an emergency permitting provision in state statute and a slew of federal disaster funds.
“They had a window in there for a while and you were able to just go and do an emergency repair,” said Skip Murray, owner of the family construction company L.P. Murray & Sons on the southern Maine coast. “I did a lot of work in municipalities in that time frame, and then that was still when you could get reimbursed” by the Federal Emergency Management Agency.
According to a rough analysis of state permit data by the Maine DEP, the number of applications for shoreline stabilization permits nearly tripled from 118 in 2022 to 313 in 2024. Department spokesperson David Madore said the state could not precisely differentiate between projects with sea walls and those without, however, he added that “most applications were for riprap stabilization”—the stone slabs and crushed rock that form the walls.
There are few state regulations on quarries in Maine, critics say, and following the recent surge, more and more towns are considering local moratoriums on new quarries, strengthened ordinances that greatly restrict the activity of existing ones, and even local restrictions on new rock sea walls.
Similar clashes among residents, quarry owners and municipal officials are unfolding beyond Gorham as towns contend with this growth and determine how best to plan for climate change and the state’s mineral needs.
A Booming Industry
There are roughly 780 active mining facilities across Maine, each excavating a unique combination of minerals and often refining or processing them on site into sand, rock, gravel and riprap for a variety of construction purposes.
From 2015 to 2021, the state saw a consistent average of three new quarry registrations per year, according to DEP mining coordinator Michael Clark, which then shot up to roughly 10 per year between 2022 and 2025, not counting a handful of expansions at existing quarries.
Clark said that he can’t be sure what’s specifically driving that trend but thought that riprap demand could be some part of it, whether it’s used for sea walls or other common uses, such as culvert construction.
Data published by the U.S. Geological Survey shows the value of crushed rock, gravel and sand produced at Maine quarries has doubled over that same period—hovering around $100 million in 2021 and a few years prior, then ballooning to more than $220 million last year.
There isn’t accompanying data on the weight or amount of construction material generating that value, but there is evidence that Maine isn’t the only New England state seeing a surge in aggregate activity.
The Massachusetts islands of Nantucket and Martha’s Vineyard have received a 125 percent increase of construction aggregate that’s been barged over the past 10 years as well as a variety of new coastal resilience projects, according to reporting from The New Bedford Light, while sand excavation sites crop up on the mainland.
Most Maine quarries are concentrated away from the coast, in towns like Gorham or Bridgton, and the state doesn’t closely regulate them beyond their pit size, blasts, dust emissions and equipment exhaust. The amount of blasting or rock crushing varies from quarry to quarry and often depends on whether there’s an obstacle of solid bedrock called ledge.
“There’s generally not blasting unless there’s a ledge,” Clark with the DEP said. “So most pits don’t have ledge. I’ve encountered some, but most do not.”
Despite that variety, many quarry neighbors have similar complaints about the quarries that do use explosives or intensive rock crushing. They describe plumes of dust and disruptive blasting operations they suspect are damaging their homes. They also complain about empty promises from quarry contractors who often refuse to share analysis of the blasts’ seismic data from their property lines. Meanwhile, there is limited oversight from municipal officials, the neighbors say.
More Blasting in Gorham?
In Gorham, Charlie Hamblen was motivated to run for town council last year by Gorham’s weak quarry ordinances and an ongoing proposal by local aggregate company Shaw Brothers Construction to expand its Brickyard Quarry near Hamblen’s home. He won the election in November 2025.
“The town was not willing to listen to the [quarry] neighbors and work on ordinances to make it a safer place for people, so I got crazy and I ran for town council,” Hamblen said.
Gorham is one of at least five Maine towns in the past two years that have received proposals for new or expanded quarries or considered adopting new ordinances to regulate them.
The town issued Shaw Brothers a permit for its 6.7-acre quarry in 2008 that allows for industrial rock crushing and an average of roughly 10 to 11 blasts per year.
Under a permit application submitted last year, the company proposed expanding the quarry to the majority of a 26-acre parcel adjacent to the existing pit and capping the number of blasts at 18 per year.
The Gorham town council rejected it in February 2025, and Shaw Brothers withdrew a subsequent request to rezone the area for industrial development, putting the project partly on hold until the company resubmitted its rezoning request earlier this summer. The Gorham planning board then unanimously recommended that the town council approve the request in early August. Now it is up to councilors to decide.
Hamblen saw the pause as the perfect opportunity for the town to explore amendments to its current mineral extraction ordinance, which has no annual limit on the number of blasts a quarry can execute so long as they meet a set of criteria. The blasts must be approved by the town, and accompanied by detailed blasting reports with seismic data made available for public view.
At the August rezoning meeting, Shaw Brothers owner Dan Shaw told the Gorham planning board that between the town’s ordinances and state regulations, the company is already “regulated to the hilt” and has addressed some environmental concerns by powering quarry operations from the energy provided by a nearby solar farm.
Maine is growing, Shaw argued, and the construction material fueling that development has to come from somewhere.
“We need quarries” for construction in Maine, Shaw added. “We need concrete. We need hospitals. We need roads.”
Shaw Brothers Construction did not respond to an interview request ahead of publication.
Hamblen and other municipal officials have been looking to the central Maine town of Winthrop for inspiration after it adopted some of the most stringent mineral extraction regulations in the state when confronted with a quarry development application in 2023. Under its updated ordinance, Winthrop now restricts the number of blasts per year, has size caps on quarry expansion requests and heightened monitoring requirements.
Voters in South Thomaston adopted similar provisions earlier this June in the aftermath of a since-rescinded expansion request from a local quarry, whose owner sits on the town planning board.
As some towns wrap up their responses to new or expanded quarry proposals, either approving restrictive ordinances or denying development permits outright, others are still receiving applications for new pits and starting from the beginning.

Residents in the town of Berwick near the New Hampshire border in southwest Maine are the latest to grapple with a new quarry proposal, this time for a 62-acre sand and gravel pit that would dispatch an average of 20 truckloads of material each day for six days a week.
Meanwhile, just 20 miles north in Alfred, the town planning board rejected a quarry proposal in August from prominent southern Maine construction and excavation company Gorham Sand & Gravel.
Each new proposal catches some towns off guard and sets others down months-long deliberations over their comprehensive plans or zoning ordinances.
Stonewalls or Wetlands
Whether this recent uptick in Maine quarries continues could be undercut by converging market forces developing outside of the aggregate industry. Earlier this summer, the Maine Department of Transportation—a massive buyer of construction aggregate of all types—announced it would be dropping up to $400 million in road construction projects after a steep budget shortfall.
Maine’s environmental agency, meanwhile, has since updated its permitting process for shoreline erosion projects to prioritize “nature-based” solutions that use plants or biodegradable materials and adds more stringent requirements for hard infrastructure like sea walls.
The rule changes respond to years of research demonstrating the collateral damage sea walls and other hard infrastructure can have on neighboring stretches of shoreline. That’s because wave energy doesn’t magically dissipate when it thrashes into plates of stone or concrete armor on the shore. Instead, the force ricochets up or down the coast and collides with beaches, bluffs or marshes that absorb the blow instead, hastening erosion in some places.
After the rush of more than 300 sea wall permits following the 2024 winter storms, the number of permits dropped back down to around 190 in 2025—close to levels before the storm.
Craig Coolidge, principal engineer and president of Maine consulting firm Summit Geoengineering, said that could be due to the additional hurdles added by the permitting rule changes, many of which now take up to nine months for approval after historically taking only six.
Since the rule changes went into effect earlier this year, Coolidge’s firm is incorporating more plantings and regenerative sediment that fills in shorelines carved away by erosion. However, he said, those “soft” approaches can’t always meet the engineering demands that armored infrastructure projects can, resulting in continued sea wall construction at a slower permitting pace.
“The vision was good, but the execution is just not there yet,” Coolidge said of the permitting changes.
Sea Wall Begets Sea Wall
Twelve miles up the coast from South Thomaston, voters in the tourist hub of Camden went a step further than the Maine DEP when they approved a 180-day moratorium on all coastal shoreline armoring projects this June in a landslide referendum.
The ban grew out of the proliferation of sea wall projects following the 2024 winter storms, said Camden planning and development coordinator Jeremy Martin, which rocked Camden especially hard due to the town’s high exposure to strong winds and storm surges.
Similar to some municipalities’ lack of quarry ordinances, Camden doesn’t have any codes on the town’s books that guide responsible sea wall development, Martin said, and the ban gives officials time to develop best practices to keep properties safe and protect the shoreline.
The current gap in oversight has led to one especially fortified stretch of riprap on a slope overlooking Sherman Cove, a scenic inlet with deep blue waters just north of Camden’s downtown. Martin said that the sheer amount of stone trucked in to build it wore down the road leading to a public boat launch.
Meanwhile, sea wall begets sea wall, causing a domino effect of Camden residents armoring their shores to protect their properties from the waves sent cascading up or down from their neighbors’ walls, according to Martin. Camden beaches and coastal habitat rely on a stable pattern of erosion to backfill the sand lost from tidal forces, but sea walls can halt erosion altogether—both good and bad.
“It impacts the natural environment, abutting property owners, and public infrastructure, and that’s why I think voters overwhelmingly approved the moratorium ordinance,” Martin said.
Martin said he understands why coastal property owners feel compelled to protect their homes and shorelines. The ordinances he and Camden officials are considering will keep that vulnerability in mind. They are likely to be modelled after another Camden ordinance Martin spearheaded that requires rigorous review for private piers and wharfs to ensure they’re built for longevity and cohesion.
Camden’s goals overlap with those of the towns seeking moratoriums and revised regulations on quarries. Both sets are trying to wrap their arms around statewide trends unspooling in their backyards before new projects are permitted and developed. Otherwise, whether it’s a quarry or sea wall, it will only have to meet the state’s requirements for permitting.
“I think the people here have decided … if there’s going to be a problem or impacts, we need to address them,” Martin said.

title: Farmers Are Going Broke Amid Rising Gas Prices, While the Ag Secretary Profits Off Them
text:
As farmers grapple with soaring diesel and fertilizer prices and the Department of Agriculture yanks support for cheaper, renewable forms of energy, the agency’s chief, Brooke Rollins, is carrying millions in highly profitable oil and gas investments.
In disclosure reports filed in July, Rollins indicated that she and her husband, Mark Rollins, an oil and gas industry executive, together hold as much as $2.5 million in fossil fuel investments. At least $1 million of that is in HKN II, a limited partnership with oil and gas interests in the Kurdistan region of Iraq; another $1 million, at least, is in Hillwood Energy New Ventures, which has interests in oil and gas operations in Texas, Rollins’ home state. Rollins also disclosed that she holds between $250,000 and $550,000 in investments in operating companies that own oil and gas assets in Texas.
Since the beginning of this year and President Donald Trump’s launch of the war in Iran, oil and gas prices have skyrocketed, and so have industry profits. Prices for diesel hit record highs this week, while prices of fertilizer, which are manufactured with natural gas and tied to the market, have also spiked this year, hitting an agriculture industry already battered by Trump’s tariffs and increasingly extreme weather events.
“Farmers have spent a billion and a half [dollars] just on additional costs for diesel because of the Iran war,” said former Washington Gov. Jay Inslee, a former presidential candidate who campaigned on progressive climate policies. “American farmers are paying through the nose for this.”
Inslee is currently working with Climate Power, a strategy and communications group that’s working to push climate and clean energy policies.
According to a Climate Power analysis, the only other top Trump administration official with significant fossil fuel investments is Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, who held as much as $320,000 in oil and gas stocks as of the end of 2025.
Trump himself has been the biggest beneficiary of his own war.
A new report from the U.S. Congress Joint Economic Committee-Minority finds that since the war sent oil and gas prices skyrocketing, the president has potentially made around $15.5 million on the oil and gas holdings he held at the end of 2025. The report says Trump owned as much as $45.6 million in oil and gas company stocks, a sum that is now worth as much as $61.1 million.
The committee noted in its report that Trump promised the industry his administration would create favorable conditions for oil and gas businesses if they donated $1 billion to his campaign. Since the launch of the war, which choked off the Strait of Hormuz, a critical passage for oil and gas from the Persian Gulf, oil and gas companies have reported more than $125 billion in profits.
“This administration is a dumpster fire of corruption and self dealing,” Inslee said. “This is just typical of an administration that is costing Americans money while they feather their own nest.”
The committee did not calculate the increase in value of Rollins’ or Clayton’s fossil fuel holdings, but Climate Power analysts project they would be similarly profitable.

Rollins is a climate skeptic who called for the repeal of the Obama administration’s landmark Clean Power Plan and for the United States to withdraw from the Paris Agreement. She was a surprise pick to lead an agency that oversees a huge range of responsibilities, including nutrition policy, agricultural subsidies, conservation programs and forest management. Though she has a degree in agricultural development and roots in farming, Rollins spent her career as a lawyer.
When Trump tapped Rollins to head the USDA, she was leading the America First Policy Institute, a group that supported Trump’s bid for a second term.
During her tenure, the agency has worked to gut a range of climate-focused programs, including redirecting millions of dollars identified for climate programs under the Biden administration’s Inflation Reduction Act.
The agency has halted funds for wind and solar projects on American farmland and disqualified renewable energy projects from loans under the Rural Energy for America Program (REAP). It also cancelled the Biden-era Partnerships for Climate-Smart Commodities program, designed to advance climate-focused practices on farms, calling it a “slush fund” for advocacy groups. And it has moved to cancel protections for millions of acres of national forest lands, which are under its purview.
The USDA did not respond to a request for an interview with Rollins.
The American Farm Bureau Federation recently projected that inflation, low commodity prices, labor and high production costs, including for diesel and fertilizer, will cost American farmers $31 billion in 2026 and $32 billion in 2027.
Farmers, as a block, have been among Trump’s most important supporters, voting overwhelmingly for him in the 2024 election. That support appears to be dissipating amid rising bankruptcies and crashing profits.
An April survey found that 94 percent of farmers were concerned about rising production costs linked to the war in Iran. The same poll found that nearly 40 percent said they were “persuadable” in the upcoming midterm elections.

title: Farmed Salmon May Not Be as Nutritious as It Once Was, New Research Suggests
text:
Eat more fatty fish.
That dietary advice has changed the way the world consumes salmon, pushing consumer demand ever upward and production to higher and higher levels. Most of that demand is being met with farmed salmon: Today, nearly 70 percent of the salmon consumed on the planet are raised in pens and cages.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Dietary Guidelines for Americans recommend eating at least 8 ounces of fish a week, and urges people to choose salmon or other species that are similarly high in “heart-healthy” Omega-3 fatty acids. But new research led by USDA scientists finds that levels of these fatty acids in farmed salmon have dropped considerably, potentially making the agency’s own advice, and similar recommendations, including from the American Heart Association, outdated and insufficient.
“These old figures are what are still used in their national dietary guidance,” said Laura Lee Cascada, director of the Aquaculture Accountability Project, a watchdog group. “So in the meantime, it’s going to stay the same and people will have this wrong idea of how much Omegas they’re getting.”
The report’s authors note in their research that the sample they examined was not large enough to require changing the government’s advice and that “a broader and more representative study is warranted.” The agency declined requests for an interview and did not answer questions via email.
The reason for the decline of the Omega-3s, the new study says, is a major shift in the diets of the naturally carnivorous salmon, from smaller fish species—which were over-exploited to feed farmed fish—to a mix that includes land-based oils and crops, including soy and canola. A 2016 study noted similar declines, also attributable to the shift toward a crop-intensive diet.
So, as the well-intended dietary advice has driven a surge in farmed salmon consumption, the corresponding surge in production appears to be depleting the very nutritional benefits that prompted the global salmon boom in the first place—and with consequences for both the marine and terrestrial environment.
Salmon has played a key role in the explosive growth of global aquaculture, becoming a mainstay in the diets of health-conscious eaters or those trying to cut down on terrestrially farmed protein, especially beef, for both health and environmental reasons. The amount of farmed salmon tripled between 2000 and 2020, far outpacing the production of any other type of finned fish.
Today aquaculture is the fastest-growing food production system in the world, much of it spurred by increasing appetites for species, including salmon, that have been identified and marketed as uniquely healthful.
But researchers and advocates have long criticized the environmental impacts of farmed salmon. Fish waste and feed pollute waters, threatening wild-caught salmon populations. Feeding ever-greater populations of pen-raised salmon has led to the degradation of both smaller fish species and the coastal fishing communities that depend on them and other wildlife, including seabirds.
With the world’s oceans becoming increasingly depleted of small fish, the industry has switched to feeding salmon a diet based more on terrestrially grown crops, including soy and soy oils.
That shift has come with a new set of problems.
Most of the world’s soy, roughly 50 percent, is grown in South America where rainforests and other climatically important ecosystems are being razed to grow feed for livestock and aquaculture.
“Soy is a major, important protein and oil ingredient in fish farming,” said Matthew Hayek, a researcher at New York University who studies the environmental impacts of protein production. “What we can tell is that, for all fish farming combined, soy consumption over the past two decades has amounted to the additional expansion and clearing of forested land that was equivalent to about the size of Nicaragua or Bangladesh.”
Hayek noted that it’s difficult to attribute soy consumption to individual fish species. But other research has found a rise in the use of crop-based ingredients fed to farmed salmon. In Norway, the world’s biggest producer of farmed salmon, 90 percent of feed ingredients were marine-based in 1990, but by 2020 that had dropped to about 23 percent. Advocacy groups there determined that 90 percent of the soy fed to farmed salmon in Norway comes from three Brazilian companies, each of which have sourced soy ingredients from illegally deforested patches of the Amazon rainforest.

Other research has found that the shift to crop-based ingredients doubled the greenhouse gas emissions, per kilogram, of farmed fish in Europe and the United Kingdom from 2000 to 2020.
“It’s trading one problem—marine exploitation—for another—land exploitation,” Cascada said.
The industry is projected to continue growing, along with the population and rising demand for seafood promoted as healthy. Nutritionists and researchers say that farmed fish, including salmon, will play a major role in providing protein, though some environmental groups note the surge in salmon demand has disproportionately come from wealthy countries that don’t have nutritional deficits.
“The claim is that the salmon industry is here to feed the world and provide this extra protein,” Cascada said. “But what it’s really doing is flooding the global north with protein that is not necessarily needed at the expense of the global South.”
In the United States, lawmakers are trying to help the industry expand by passing legislation that would make it easier for salmon producers to obtain licenses to farm fish in offshore federal waters.
In February, environmental advocates and fishermen sent a letter to members of Congress opposing the bill, the Marine Aquaculture Research for America (MARA) Act.
Proponents of the bill say that putting fish farms in deeper, offshore waters would reduce the environmental issues caused by farming fish in sensitive, nearshore environments.
Opponents say the legislation would enable a factory-farming model, much like the one that produces the vast majority of the world’s livestock, in the open sea.

title: Climate ‘Overshoot’ Is Coming—Are We Ready?
text:
Fossil fuel emissions are pushing Earth’s climate toward a dangerous new phase of climate “overshoot,” scientists warned Wednesday in a new report from the United Nations Environmental Programme.
The report, Limiting Overshoot, projects that global temperatures will exceed the 1.5-degree Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warming threshold identified in the Paris Agreement within a few years, intensifying deadly climate impacts. It says the best chance of restoring a safe climate is to begin cutting greenhouse gas emissions immediately, halve them by 2035, and figure out ways to remove billions of tons of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere before the end of the century.
The 1.5 degrees of warming identified in the report and the Paris pact refers to the increase in global temperatures since the preindustrial period of 1850 to 1900, before humans altered the atmosphere and climate with billions of tons of fossil fuel emissions and other industrial and agricultural pollution.
Under the 2015 agreement, more than 190 countries pledged to keep the global temperature below that level because they knew warming above that would mean even greater intensification of extreme weather events, ecosystem losses and the potential submersion of small island countries.
Multiple scientific studies, including global assessments from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, project that warming of more than 1.5 degrees Celsius will cause severe damage to human health, food and water supplies, as well as infrastructure and economies.
Scientists have calculated that at the current pace of emissions, warming could reach a catastrophic 2.7 to 3 degrees Celsius by 2100. If all the measures promised by governments under the Paris Agreement are implemented, warming could be limited to about 1.7 or 1.8 degrees Celsius, which would make it easier to return below the 1.5-degree Celsius threshold.
If Earth’s fever stays in the ‘overshoot’ zone too long, it could push ice sheets and key heat-carrying ocean currents past tipping points “that become difficult or impossible to reverse on human timescales,” the report concludes.
“We must make the overshoot as small and short as possible, limiting how high temperatures rise and how long they remain above 1.5 degrees Celsius,” said United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres.
The new report, he added, identifies a triple play of climate action: accelerating the phaseout of fossil fuels and the transition to renewable energy, slashing methane pollution and protecting climate allies, such as lands, forests and oceans, that take heat-trapping carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere.
“We’ve failed to act on the options that were available 15 or 20 years ago to reduce emissions rapidly,” said report co-author Joeri Rogelj, a climate scientist at the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis in Austria and a professor at Imperial College London. “The reality is that we have failed in that endeavor, and it needs to be acknowledged.”
The new report does just that, and it is alarming because the climate impacts projected for warming above 1.5 degrees Celsius are “unacceptable or unbearable for at least the poorest and the most vulnerable communities around the world,” he said. This summer, with heatwaves that killed thousands in Europe and burned parts of towns in North America, showed that developed countries in the Global North are not immune, he added.
“We need to face the consequences of this failure by dealing with the unavoidable impact,” he said. He added that there is a wide gap between doing nothing by allowing warming to continue for the rest of the century, and acting now to limit the peak temperature and the length of time the global temperatures remain above the threshold.
Co-author Carl-Friedrich Schleussner, another climate researcher at IIASA, said the report doesn’t just document the state of the global climate. Given the climate impacts happening at about 1.4 degrees Celsius warming, he said the report is “more about what it means for us here now, and what the response needs to look like.”
As warming heats the planet at the rate of half a degree Celsius every 20 years, he said “extreme events and climate-driven natural disasters are increasingly exceeding the capacities of ecosystems and of human systems.”
This summer’s extremes show this happening now, not in the distant future, he said, with extreme heat in Europe hitting places where it’s been rare and overwhelming the adaptive capacity of hospitals, schools and retirement homes. Extreme heat contributed to about 15,000 heat-related deaths in Germany, one of the most developed countries in the world.
“We are seeing what it entails to adapt to climate change, and we are seeing that we have an enormous gap,” Schleussner said. “We are really lagging behind. We are not prepared for what’s coming.”

title: Why Montana Firefighters Are Intentionally Burning Areas Around Two Wildfires
text:
About a month ago, two wildfires ignited a day apart in southwest Montana. The Bobcat Lakes Fire started July 31 near Wise River, followed by the Sand Creek Fire on Aug. 1 near Wisdom.
Now, crews working to contain them are intentionally setting fire to vegetation in areas where steep, densely timbered terrain makes direct attack too dangerous.
The tactic, known as strategic firing, is being used where crews cannot safely work directly along portions of the active fire edge. Firefighters work from roads, trails or control lines they’ve dug and intentionally burn vegetation between those lines and the main fire. The U.S. Forest Service describes this type of burnout operation as an indirect firefighting tactic used to help contain wildfires.
On Aug. 31, crews conducted firing operations on the northwest side of the Sand Creek Fire. The operations increased smoke production, according to the incident management team. Cold air and southeasterly winds caused smoke to settle into the Big Hole Valley overnight and into the following morning.
Mariah Leuschen-Lonergan, fire communications lead for the U.S. Forest Service’s Northern Rockies Fire & Aviation Management program, said some sections of the Sand Creek and Bobcat Lakes fires are burning in steep, densely timbered terrain that is difficult for firefighters to safely enter and leave.
Intentionally burning vegetation between the fires “removes the fuel before the main fire gets there, so when the fire edge reaches the burned-out area, there’s nothing left to carry it forward,” Leuschen-Lonergan said in an email response to Inside Climate News.
She said the approach gives crews a safer place to work and can help protect private property in the path of the fire.
Firefighters consider safety and threatened property or infrastructure when deciding whether to use a firing operation, Leuschen-Lonergan said.
Terrain, vegetation, current fire behavior and weather also influence where and when the operations are conducted.
“Firing is one tool among several for building and securing control lines,” she said.
Fire officials have not specified how much of the reported 45,561 acres burned by both fires resulted from strategic firing operations.
Fire officials said they are working on a very rough estimate and will share it as soon as possible.They confirmed that acres burned during firing operations are included in the reported total acreage of each fire.
On the Sand Creek Fire, crews have been using a combination of direct and indirect control lines. Along the western side, firefighters were preparing the Steel-Fox Road as a control line and using hand firing operations to burn pockets of heavy fuels and bring that fire toward established control lines, according to the latest incident update.
Large amounts of dead and downed timber in the southwest portion of the blaze has challenged firefighters. Fire officials said the probability of holding a control line there was very low, prompting crews to scout locations to dig control lines away from the active fire edge, where firefighters could work more safely.
Leuschen-Lonergan said fire managers, in deciding when to intentionally burn downed limbs and vegetation, examine temperature, humidity, wind speed and direction and the moisture level of available fuels, including grass, needles, twigs, branches and brush, as well as heavier logs on the ground.
An incident meteorologist assigned to the fire provides forecasts for the specific location. Fire behavior analysts, operations personnel and the meteorologist evaluate the conditions before a firing operation is approved and carried out.
“No two fires, or even two spots on the same fire, are identical,” Leuschen-Lonergan said.
Crews conduct firing operations when conditions allow vegetation to burn at an intensity they can manage. Wind direction and speed are monitored during the operation to reduce the possibility that the fire will move toward homes or increase in intensity.
If conditions are not suitable, the operation does not proceed.
Rain can also affect the operations. If fuels become too wet to burn effectively, crews may postpone the work until conditions change.

Leuschen-Lonergan said the challenges are not limited to firing operations.
“It’s not firing operations specifically that are getting harder, it’s fire operations in general, and there are many elements involved in those challenges,” she said.
“Fire seasons seem to be running longer. Fuel loads and standing dead trees are heavier in many areas, which makes direct attack, usually our safest option, harder to use.”
She said those conditions can result in greater reliance on suppression methods that keep firefighters farther away from the wildfire.
“We lean on indirect tactics like firing operations more often,” she said.
Development in wooded areas is another factor, Leuschen-Lonergan said, reducing the number of locations where firefighters can safely engage a fire.
Weather conditions could present additional challenges for firefighters in southwest Montana.
The Sept. 1 incident update forecast high temperatures of between 73 and 79 degrees and minimum relative humidity between 19 and 24 percent. Thunderstorms were expected during the afternoon and evening.
Fire activity was expected to increase because of dry air and atmospheric instability, according to the incident management team. Much of the heat on the Sand Creek Fire remained on its western side.
Weather conditions also affect whether strategic firing operations can proceed. Strong or shifting winds can cause crews to postpone or stop an operation, while rain can make fuels too wet to burn as intended.
“The firing operation is intended to be lower intensity than an uncontrolled run of the main fire,” Leuschen-Lonergan said. “That difference in intensity is what makes it a protective tool rather than an added risk.”
